text: A Scheduled Job lives in the sysauto_script table, and it runs on a clock, not because a record changed. Where a Business Rule wakes up for one specific record event, right as that event happens, a Scheduled Job wakes up because the time arrived, with no record involved at all.

And when a Scheduled Job runs, it's usually built to sweep across many records at once, rather than acting on just one. The Run field gives real scheduling options: a specific time once a day, a repeat interval like every 30 minutes, or a more flexible recurring pattern similar to a cron schedule for jobs needing particular days.

Whichever option is chosen, the job record also tracks Next action, which tells you exactly when it's due to fire next — your first stop whenever someone asks whether a job actually ran, and how its run history compares against what you'd expect given its configured interval.

Three real jobs worth knowing. SLA recalculation jobs re-evaluate SLA records in bulk against current time and business rules, catching breaches rather than recalculating on every single record change. Scheduled reports generate and email themselves on a recurring schedule instead of a user pulling them manually. And housekeeping jobs purge old data — including a real example that trims old rows out of the system log table.

The distinction that matters: a Business Rule is reactive, tied to a specific event, before or after insert, update, or delete, on a specific record. A Scheduled Job is proactive on a timer, firing because a clock expired regardless of whether any record changed, and often operating across a whole set of records in one pass.

Finding all SLAs due to breach in the next hour is a Scheduled Job's kind of task — nobody edited a record to trigger that check. As an admin, check Next action and run history first if a job seems to be missing runs or running too long. Next up: the System Log application.
